opus-5.5.text:
So the main reason is diversity. When you're generating synthetic data with a language model, one of the biggest failure modes is that the model collapses toward a narrow set of outputs. If you keep giving it the same few in-context examples, it tends to anchor on them pretty heavily. You get problems that look structurally similar, use the same kinds of numbers, the same story templates, the same reasoning patterns, just with surface details swapped out. And that's not very useful for training, because the downstream model ends up seeing a lot of near-duplicates rather than a genuinely broad distribution of problems.

So by rotating the examples, and sometimes drawing them from the pool of problems we've already generated in earlier rounds, we're nudging the generator into different regions of the problem space each time. It's a bit like seeding the model's imagination differently on every iteration. One round it might see a combinatorics-flavored example and a geometry one, the next round something about rates or modular arithmetic, and that shifts what it produces.

There's also a second benefit, which is that you can steer difficulty and novelty that way. If you feed back examples that are a little harder or a little more unusual than the seed set, the generator tends to stretch toward that. So over iterations you can get a kind of gradual expansion, both in coverage and in challenge, rather than just regurgitating what was in the original handful of human-written examples.

And honestly, part of the broader lesson for us has been that with synthetic data, quantity alone doesn't buy you much. What really matters is the diversity and the quality of what you generate. Varying the prompts is one fairly simple but surprisingly effective lever for getting that diversity, and then of course you still need filtering and verification on top, because the model will happily generate problems that are ill-posed or have wrong answers if you're not careful.

r001.rationale: The response says examples may come from problems generated in earlier rounds, but does not say those examples came from a filtering stage.

r002.rationale: It explains that rotating varied examples nudges the model into different regions of the problem space and describes this as seeding its imagination differently.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we learned pretty quickly the hard way. When you ask a language model to generate math problems, it has strong priors, and those priors are mode-seeking. If you give it the same few in-context examples every time, you'll see the same templates come back over and over. Different numbers, different names, but structurally it's the same problem. Trains leaving stations, apples being shared among friends. And if you measure diversity, like embedding similarity or even just n-gram overlap, it collapses fast.

So the examples in the prompt act as a kind of anchor, and the model doesn't drift very far from that anchor on its own. By rotating the examples, we're essentially moving the anchor around. Each iteration we pull a fresh set of seed problems, sometimes from different sources, different difficulty levels, different subdomains, so the model is being conditioned on a different region of the problem space each time. That gives you much broader coverage than just sampling at high temperature, which tends to buy you noise more than genuine novelty.

The other piece is that we're often doing this iteratively, where problems generated in one round can feed back as examples for the next. If you're not careful, that becomes a feedback loop where whatever quirks the model has get amplified. So we deliberately mix in new human-written examples and filter for diversity before anything goes back into the prompt. It keeps the distribution from narrowing on itself.

And honestly, it matters a lot for what you're training downstream. If the synthetic data is secretly a few thousand variations of a dozen templates, the student model learns the templates, not the reasoning. Changing the examples is a cheap intervention, but it's one of the more effective ones we found for actually getting the long tail.

r001.rationale: It says problems generated in one round can feed back as examples for the next, after mixing in new examples and filtering for diversity.

r002.rationale: It explains that rotating to fresh examples from different sources, difficulty levels, and subdomains moves the model’s anchor and broadens coverage.

astra-6.text: If you keep using the same examples, the model tends to generate problems that look very similar to those examples. It might change the numbers or the names, but the underlying reasoning stays the same. So we change the examples across iterations to encourage more diversity in the problems and the reasoning they require. Otherwise, you can generate a lot of data without actually adding much new information.

r001.rationale: The response says examples change across iterations, but does not say they come from earlier generation and filtering.

r002.rationale: It says changing examples across iterations is intended to encourage more diverse problems and reasoning, conveying the purpose of giving the model fresh inspiration.

sol-6.1.text: The examples in the prompt influence what the model generates. If we keep using the same examples, it tends to produce variations of those same problems. By changing the examples across iterations, we encourage a broader range of problems and reasoning patterns, so the synthetic data becomes more diverse.
